raw_case_text:
A 23-year-old female initially presented with a 2-month history of severe frontal sinus headaches and upward gaze diplopia. She had no other significant medical issues and denied nasal symptoms. An outside magnetic resonance imaging scan of her brain was obtained that showed a left ethmoid mass measuring 2.4 x 2.3 x 2.5 cm extending into the left frontal sinus. A computed tomography sinus was then done in the office that revealed an expansile mass destroying the left lamina papyracea and fiberoptic laryngoscopy demonstrated a mass in the posterior nasopharynx adjacent to the left orbit and posterior to the left middle turbinate (Figure 1).
She was taken emergently to the operating room for functional endoscopic sinus surgery (ESS) under COVID restrictions and the frontal ethmoid mucocele was completely decompressed. A culture of the left frontal sinus was taken and did not show any fungal organisms. The patient then performed daily nasal saline irrigations and presented to postoperative appointments with mild orbital pain that decreased in intensity with each subsequent visit. Monthly nasal endoscopies consistently revealed an open, wide area at the site of the decompressed mucocele for three consecutive months. Three weeks later, she called the surgeon (N.L.S.) one Saturday night complaining of sudden onset, sharp pain that felt like she had a "knife in her left eye." She was treated conservatively over the weekend with nasal irrigations and a nasal corticosteroid spray. A video endoscopy in the office revealed a sharp object penetrating the left orbital tissue (Figure 2). Attempted removal under video endoscopy failed and was painful as the spicule was impacted into the periorbital tissue that was now unprotected because the bony lamina papyracea had been resorbed by pressure from the mucocele. The object was finally irrigated under general anesthesia in the operating room. Spicule fragments were cultured and sent to pathology. Both reports were consistent with Aspergillus fumigatus. The patient's "knife-like" pain was relieved after the procedure, but orbital pressure persisted until the fungal infection was brought under control.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 23-year-old female presented with a 2-month history of severe frontal sinus headaches and upward gaze diplopia, followed postoperatively by sudden-onset sharp knife-like left eye pain.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient initially developed severe frontal sinus headaches and upward gaze diplopia over 2 months without nasal symptoms. After emergent functional endoscopic sinus surgery (ESS) to decompress a left fronto-ethmoid mucocele, she performed daily nasal saline irrigations and experienced mild orbital pain that progressively improved over 3 consecutive monthly follow-up visits. Three weeks after her third monthly visit, she experienced sudden-onset sharp pain described as feeling like a knife in her left eye, which did not resolve with weekend conservative therapy using nasal saline irrigations and nasal corticosteroid spray.
subjective.past_medical_history: No significant prior medical issues; underwent functional endoscopic sinus surgery (ESS) for left fronto-ethmoid mucocele decompression.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for severe frontal sinus headache, upward gaze diplopia, and subsequent acute sharp left orbital pain; negative for nasal symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: Initial office fiberoptic laryngoscopy demonstrated a mass in the posterior nasopharynx adjacent to the left orbit and posterior to the left middle turbinate. Postoperative monthly nasal endoscopies for 3 months showed a wide, open decompressed mucocele cavity. Subsequent office video endoscopy during acute pain revealed a sharp spicule penetrating the unprotected left periorbital tissue where the bony lamina papyracea had been resorbed; attempted in-office removal was painful and unsuccessful.
objective.advanced_workup: Initial outside brain MRI showed a left ethmoid mass measuring 2.4 x 2.3 x 2.5 cm extending into the left frontal sinus. Office sinus CT revealed an expansile mass destroying the left lamina papyracea. Initial intraoperative left frontal sinus culture at ESS showed no fungal organisms. Following operating room irrigation and removal of the penetrating orbital spicule under general anesthesia, pathology and fungal culture of the spicule fragments were both positive for Aspergillus fumigatus.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Left fronto-ethmoid mucocele complicated by secondary orbital/sinonasal Aspergillus fumigatus infection with a fungal spicule penetrating the periorbital tissue through a resorbed lamina papyracea, confirmed by histopathology and fungal culture of extracted spicule fragments. Treated initially with emergent functional endoscopic sinus surgery, daily saline irrigations, and nasal corticosteroid spray, followed by operating room irrigation and spicule removal under general anesthesia and targeted antifungal therapy. Knife-like pain resolved immediately after surgical removal, and residual orbital pressure resolved once the Aspergillus fumigatus infection was controlled.
